How PolitiDex works ▾

PolitiDex is a free, nonpartisan record of what politicians say and how they actually vote. Look up anyone, check a claim against the roll call behind it, and see the sourced receipts either way.

Checking the receipts yourself takes hours, so most of us end up voting on party or gut feeling. PolitiDex does that homework year-round — and when an election comes, it turns the record into a voting team of the people who earned it.

🧭 Let your values be your True North

Don't judge them by their party.
Judge them by your values.

Tell PolitiDex the positions you actually believe in — that's your True North. Where a politician's record runs deep enough to test, you get a personal Your Match %: a clear, sourced read of how their record lines up with yours, red or blue. Where it doesn't, you get the record and no percentage — the same floor the rest of the site holds. It is read off the same receipts as everything else here — their votes, against your positions.

Free · Nonpartisan · Takes about a minute

PolitiDex resolves your U.S. Senate and Governor seats from your state, anywhere in the country. Your U.S. House, State Senate and State House seats need district lines, which we map in Utah so far — elsewhere we leave those rows blank rather than name someone else’s district. Local offices — mayor, council, school board, county — are listed where we have them, and we say so where we don’t. A blank row is not a dead end: anyone, anywhere, can read the record of everyone we track from the chamber-and-state listings below — those are archive listings, not seats.

BUILD YOUR VOTING TEAM

This is where the record becomes a ballot. Your ballot has more than one seat — U.S. Senate, U.S. House, Governor, your statehouse, and local offices. For each seat PolitiDex can resolve for you, it opens the field on the formal record so you can pick the candidate who actually shares your values and follows through — then saves your team so it's ready on election day. Where a seat needs district lines we don't draw yet, it says so instead of filling in a stranger.

“Which party am I?”

Vote the whole ticket by the letter next to each name — and hope they earn it.

★ Community Submitted · A Citizen Voice ★

Community Evidence Exchange

A space for the community to surface evidence, topics, and issues that may have been missed. Post a lead, discuss it, and let quality reactions push the strongest ones to the top.

📌 This is a separate discussion layer. Posts here are not part of the curated Evidence Locker and are clearly marked “Community Submitted.” The strongest, best-sourced posts can be suggested for review and manually promoted by a moderator.

🗣 Looking to just talk it out? The Open Discussion board is the free-conversation track — post anything, vote, and reply, with no verification bar. This Exchange is the verified track; the Open board is the open one, and the two never mix.

How it works Discover → Compare → Build your team
1 Discover Look anyone up Search or filter the list below by office, state or party to pull up anyone in the record. Working out your ballot? Start at — it names your seats and opens the field for each one.
→
2 Compare Put 2–4 side by side Tap ⚖️ Compare on any cards, then open the table to weigh records, promises and policy positions head-to-head. Comparing the candidates for one seat side-by-side is the fastest way to decide that race.
→
3 Decide Add your pick to your team Right inside the comparison, hit ⭐ Add to Team to claim that seat on your saved 2026 ballot.

💡 Reading the records together: 🏛️ Official Record is how they voted, and ⚖️ Word vs Action is whether that record backs what they said — including any campaign pledges, which are measured the same way as every other stated position rather than ranked on their own. The 🎯 Alignment Tool shows how all of that lands on your issues.

🔒 ADMIN: Politician Manager

POLITICIAN MANAGER

Search, filter, create, edit, and clean up the live politician database. Track database coverage to spot missing Utah seats and offices, flag duplicates, promote stubs to full profiles, and add new records — all writing directly to Firestore, no re-import required.

⚡ Quick Add / Paste JSON

Paste a single politician object or an array of many. Each record is matched to an existing profile by id first, then by name — matches are updated (your fields merged in), everything else is created. All changes are written to Firestore in one batch.

Accepted format & fields
Supported shapes: a single { … } object, an array [ { … }, { … } ], or a keyed map { "id": { … } }.
Common fields: id, name, office, district, state, party, tier, icon, photo, bio, quote, quoteSource, keyIssues, stances, score, promises, accountability, spotlight.
keyIssues may be an array or newline-separated text. stances and accountability are merged onto any existing values; other fields overwrite. Only name is required for a new record.
spotlight is the optional personal-integrity layer — public statements, conduct and notable actions that show whether an official's words match their actions, kept deliberately separate from promises (formal in-office votes/bills/pledges that drive Promise %). Provide 3–5 summarized highlights, e.g. [{ "headline": "…", "facts": "…", "why": "…", "date": "2024", "impact": "negative", "category": "redflags", "source": { "label": "Reuters", "url": "https://…" } }]. Entries with impact set to "positive" (words match actions) or "negative" (reversal/inconsistency/controversy) are tagged as Accountability Score drivers: they move the integrity score, appear under “Spotlight items feeding this score” in the Accountability card, and tap back and forth between the two sections. category may match an accountability key (promise, voting, rhetoric, redflags, transparency) to label which part of the score the item touches. source is an optional { label, url } rendered as a linked citation on the item. Set impact to "neutral" to show an item as context explicitly marked “no score impact”; entries with no impact appear as recent news.
📊 Database Coverage & Missing Politicians

A live map of what's in the database versus what should exist. Utah's legislative seats and statewide offices are tracked seat-by-seat — click any missing seat to start a pre-filled new record.

🎚 What the money lane reports — and what it refuses to

This lane reports composition, not a grade. For each person with an itemized filing it shows the dollars in each bucket the FEC itself reports, that bucket's share of the itemized base, and the largest reported source named as a fact about a sorted list. There is no 0–100 number, no level and no letter — the "Constituents-First signal" that used to sit here has been retired, arithmetic and all.

Sourcing is disclosure-based: itemized public filings (FEC for federal offices, Utah's disclosure system for state and local), split into the FEC's own buckets. Outside ("dark-money") spending is reported at the level the filing supports and never as a dollar figure, because outside spending is not itemized to the candidate. No motive is inferred anywhere. A filing shows where money came from. It does not show why anyone voted for anything, and this lane never says it does.

Coverage, stated up front. Itemized filings are on file for a small minority of the people PolitiDex carries, and every profile says so. Where a filing is missing that is missing data — it is not a finding about the person, and no surface reads it as one.

The wall. Nothing on this lane is an input to Direction Match, to ⚖️ Word vs Action, to a formal pattern tier, to the publication floor, to any count of formal acts, to Your Match, or to any ordering of one person against another. It is a separate lane and it ends where it is printed.

I

Foundations — How Power Is Built

Start here: the machinery of American government, top to bottom.

01
🏛️
Foundations⏱️ 3 min read

How the U.S. Government Works

Three branches, one system of checks & balances.

+

The Founders deliberately split power so no single person or group could control everything. Government is divided into three branches, and each one can check the other two.

⚖️ Legislative

Makes the laws. Congress = the House + the Senate. It writes and passes bills, controls federal spending (the "power of the purse"), declares war, and confirms or rejects key appointments.

🏛️ Executive

Enforces the laws. The President, Vice President, Cabinet, and federal agencies. Signs or vetoes bills, runs the military, conducts foreign policy, and nominates judges & officials.

🧑‍⚖️ Judicial

Interprets the laws. The Supreme Court and lower federal courts. Decides whether laws are constitutional, settles disputes, and sets binding precedent for the future.

🗺️ Federalism

Power is split again. The federal government handles national matters; states keep everything not handed to D.C. — which is why the same issue can be legal in one state and banned in another.

🔄Checks & balances in action: Congress passes a law → the President can veto it → Congress can override that veto with a 2/3 vote → and the courts can still strike the law down if it violates the Constitution.
🏛️ USA.gov: Branches 📜 Founding Documents
🎯Why this matters to you: When a candidate promises something, ask first — does that office even have the power to do it? Half of all campaign promises die on that question alone.
02
🪪
Foundations⏱️ 3 min read

What Each Office Actually Controls

Who has real power over what — from D.C. to your county.

+

Knowing what a position can and can't do is how you hold the right person accountable — and how you spot a promise that office has no power to keep.

👤 President

Enforces federal law, sets foreign policy & treaties, commands the military, vetoes bills, and nominates judges. Cannot pass laws or set the budget alone.

🏛️ U.S. Senate

100 members (2 per state, 6-year terms). Confirms judges & Cabinet, ratifies treaties, and holds impeachment trials. Every state gets an equal voice.

🗳️ U.S. House

435 members (by population, 2-year terms). Originates spending & tax bills, represents local districts, and starts the impeachment process.

📨 Your Representative

Your direct line into federal lawmaking — the federal official closest to your community's day-to-day needs.

🏔 Governor

The state's chief executive. Signs or vetoes state laws, proposes the state budget, commands the National Guard, and runs state agencies (DMV, schools, roads).

🏙️ Mayor & City Council

Local power: police, zoning, parks, local roads, and city budgets — the decisions you feel most directly.

📍Reality check: Many things that shape daily life — schools, policing, zoning, local roads — are decided at the state and local level, not in Washington.
🔎 Find Your Officials 🗺️ Open Your Power Map
🎯Aim your energy: Frustrated about potholes or school policy? That's a city-council or governor fight — not a presidential one. Hold the right office accountable.
03
📜
Foundations⏱️ 3 min read

How a Bill Becomes Law

From a single idea to the law of the land — step by step.

+

Most bills never make it. Here's the full gauntlet a proposal has to survive to become law:

  1. Introduction. A member of Congress drafts a bill and introduces it in the House or the Senate.
  2. Committee review. A specialized committee studies it, holds hearings, amends it — or quietly lets it die.
  3. Floor debate & vote. The full chamber debates, amends, and votes. It needs a majority to move forward.
  4. The other chamber. The second chamber repeats the whole process. Both must pass identical text (differences are settled in a conference committee).
  5. The President's desk. Sign it → it's law. Veto it → it goes back. Ignore it 10 days while Congress is in session → it becomes law anyway.
  6. Override (if vetoed). Congress can still pass it over a veto with a 2/3 vote in both chambers.
  7. Law & the courts. Agencies enforce it — and courts can later rule it unconstitutional.
💡Why it matters: A politician "introducing" or "fighting for" a bill is not the same as that bill becoming law. Watch where it actually died.
📜 Congress.gov: The Process 🔎 Track Live Bills
📑Next up: Knowing the process is step one — Lesson 04 shows you how to crack open the bill's actual text and find what it really does.
II

Decode the Documents — Read Past the Headlines

The skills to read a bill, a promise, and a news story for what they really say.

04
📑
New Lesson⏱️ 4 min read

How to Read a Bill

Crack open the actual text and find what it really does.

+

A bill's real meaning lives in its text, not its title. A law named the "Freedom & Prosperity Act" might do neither. Here's how to read one like a staffer instead of a headline.

🔖 Bill Number

Like H.R. 1 (House) or S. 1 (Senate) — the tracking number you'll use to follow it anywhere.

✍️ Sponsors & Cosponsors

Who introduced it and who signed on. Whose names are attached tells you whose priorities it serves.

📃 Findings & Purpose

The "why" section up top — and where spin hides. Read the stated goals skeptically.

🧩 The Operative Sections

The real rules. "Shall" means mandatory; "may" means optional. Tiny words, huge difference.

💵 Appropriations

How much money, to whom, for how long. Follow the dollars to find the real intent.

📅 Effective & Sunset Dates

When it kicks in — and whether it quietly expires later.

🪤Watch for riders & "poison pills": unrelated provisions slipped into a must-pass bill so they ride through without a vote of their own.
📊Pro move: never trust the summary alone — read the CBO score for the true cost, then skim the sections that actually change the law.
📑 Read Bill Text 📖 Legislative Glossary 💵 CBO Cost Estimates
05
🎭
Decode⏱️ 3 min read

Reading Promises vs Reality

Cut through the talking points and spot the spin.

+

Politicians are trained to sound good. These habits help you separate what was actually done from what was merely said.

🎯 Watch the verb

"Fought for," "supported," "called for" ≠ "passed," "signed," "delivered." Vague verbs hide inaction.

🗳️ Vote, not the speech

A floor speech is free. Look at the recorded vote and the final outcome instead.

📅 Follow the timeline

Did the result happen because of them — or was it already in motion before they arrived?

🔢 Find the number

"Massive investment" is spin. "$2.1B over 5 years" is a fact you can verify.

🔗 Find the source

Real claims link to bills, budgets, or records. No source = treat it as opinion.

🥊 Beware the strawman

If they only attack "the other side," they may be dodging their own record.

✅Put it to work: PolitiDex checks every claim against the record — one Word vs Action read with the receipts behind it — check it yourself instead of taking anyone's word.
🧾One-line test: "Did they vote for it, fund it, and sign it?" If you can't answer all three, the promise isn't kept — it's just a soundbite.
📊 Open the Promise Tracker 🔎 PolitiFact
06
📺
New Lesson⏱️ 4 min read

Understanding Media Spin

Every story is framed by someone — learn to see the frame.

+

News isn't just facts — it's facts chosen, ordered, and packaged. Spin isn't always lying; it's steering what you notice. Learn these moves and you can read any outlet, left or right.

🪧 Framing

Which detail leads? What's buried in paragraph 12? The order of a story is an argument.

🔥 Loaded language

"Slammed," "blasted," "regime." Emotion-words do persuasion the facts can't.

📉 Cherry-picked stats

A true number with no baseline or context can be twisted to prove almost anything.

📰 Headline ≠ story

Headlines are built to be shared; the body often quietly walks them back.

🕶️ Anonymous sources

"Sources say" can be real — or convenient. Ask who benefits from the leak.

⚖️ False balance

Giving "both sides" equal weight when the evidence isn't equal is its own bias.

🧭Outrage is the business model: content engineered to make you angry keeps you scrolling. Pause before you share.
🔗The fix: trace it to the primary source — the actual bill, study, or transcript — and read across several outlets before you decide.
⚖️ AllSides Bias Ratings ✅ FactCheck.org 📰 Media Bias Check
III

Follow the Money — Who Really Pays

How campaigns are funded, and the warning signs that money is buying a vote.

07
💰
Follow the Money⏱️ 3 min read

Campaign Finance & Wealth Transparency

Follow the money behind the message.

+

Campaigns run on money, and who funds a politician can shape who they answer to. Transparency is how voters see those ties. Know the key terms:

🏦 PAC

A Political Action Committee — raises money to support candidates within legal donation limits.

🚀 Super PAC

Can raise and spend unlimited sums independently, but can't donate directly to a candidate.

🌑 Dark Money

Funds from groups that don't have to disclose who their donors are.

🎁 Bundling

One person gathering many separate donations to amplify their influence.

🤵 Lobbying

Paid efforts to influence how legislators write and vote on laws.

📋 Disclosure

Public FEC reports showing who gave, how much, and when.

🔎Why wealth matters: Financial disclosures and net-worth tracking can reveal conflicts of interest — like voting on industries a lawmaker is personally invested in.
💡Follow the chain: donor → committee → vote. When all three line up against the public interest, you've found a story worth telling.
💰 Follow the Money 📈 Wealth Leaderboard 🔗 OpenSecrets
08
🚩
New Lesson⏱️ 4 min read

Red Flags in Campaign Finance

Spot the warning signs of money buying influence.

+

Money in politics is legal — but certain patterns are smoke that often signals fire. None of these prove corruption on their own. Together, they're worth a very hard look.

  • A donation right before a vote. A big check from an industry just days before a lawmaker votes on its bill.
  • Votes that match the donor, not the district. A position that helps funders but few actual constituents.
  • The revolving door. A politician or their staff who leaves office to lobby the very agency they once oversaw.
  • Last-minute dark money. Untraceable ad spending that floods in during the final weeks of a race.
  • Leadership-PAC luxury spending. "Campaign" funds spent on resorts, fine dining, and travel.
  • One mega-donor, many committees. Maxing out to a candidate, their PAC, and a Super PAC to multiply influence.
🔎Correlation isn't proof — it's a question. Cross-check the donation date against the vote date, then ask why the timing lines up.
🕵️Do it yourself: pull a politician's top donors on OpenSecrets, then compare them to their committee assignments. The overlap is where to dig.
💰 Follow the Money 🔗 OpenSecrets 📋 FEC Filings
IV

Know Your Rights — Your Power at the Ballot

The freedoms the republic guarantees you, and how to defend your vote.

09
🦅
Your Rights⏱️ 3 min read

The Constitution & Your Rights

The rulebook of the republic — and the rights it guarantees you.

+

Ratified in 1788, the Constitution is the supreme law of the land. It builds the three branches, divides power between the federal government and the states, and — through the Bill of Rights (the first 10 amendments) — guarantees individual freedoms. There are 27 amendments in all.

🗣️ 1st Amendment

Freedom of speech, religion, press, assembly, and the right to petition the government.

🔫 2nd Amendment

The right to keep and bear arms.

🔍 4th Amendment

Protection from unreasonable searches and seizures.

⚖️ 5th Amendment

Due process, no self-incrimination, and protection from double jeopardy.

🤝 14th Amendment

Equal protection and due process under the law for all citizens.

🗳️ 15th · 19th · 26th

Voting rights protected regardless of race, sex, and for everyone 18 and older.

🛡️Hard to change by design: Amending the Constitution takes 2/3 of Congress and 3/4 of the states — so your rights can't be erased on a whim.
📜Keep it close: the whole document is a short read. Knowing what it actually says is the surest defense against anyone who tells you it says otherwise.
🦅 Read the Constitution 📜 Bill of Rights
10
🗳️
New Lesson⏱️ 4 min read

Your Rights as a Voter

Know exactly what you're entitled to at the ballot box.

+

Your right to vote is protected by law — but the rules vary by state, and knowing them is how you make sure your vote actually counts.

✅ Right to register

Every eligible citizen can register. Many states now offer online or same-day registration.

🪪 ID rules vary

Some states require photo ID, others don't. Check your state's rule before election day.

🗳️ Provisional ballot

If your eligibility is questioned, you can still cast a provisional ballot that's verified later.

⏰ Time off to vote

Many states legally require employers to give you paid or unpaid time off to vote.

🤝 Right to assistance

Voters with disabilities or language needs can get help; accessible and curbside voting exist.

🚫 Freedom from intimidation

No one may threaten, harass, or block you from voting. Voter intimidation is a federal crime.

⚠️Turned away or name missing? Ask for a provisional ballot — never just leave. Then call the nonpartisan Election Protection hotline at 866-OUR-VOTE.
📅Deadlines win elections: registration cutoffs, mail-ballot request dates, and drop-off times all vary. Confirm yours early — don't get caught out.

PolitiDex is neutral by design, community-powered, and has no agenda except accountability. Here's how everyday citizens hold elected officials to their word.

Citizens dig into the public record — campaign speeches, floor votes, press conferences, and official filings. Every submission requires a verifiable source link, ensuring nothing enters the system unchecked.

2. VERIFY

The community reviews and votes on every claim. Evidence is cross-referenced against nonpartisan, publicly available records. Disputes are escalated to a volunteer editorial board with full transparency at every step.

Verified claims update each politician's Word vs Action read and pledge receipts in real time. No rumors, no spin, no partisan weighting — just a clear, data-driven record of who keeps their word and who doesn't. The result: accountability you can measure.

Word vs Action

The one graded read on PolitiDex
The question, asked the same way on every profile
Does what they say match what they do?

WORD is everything they have documented and sourced — not only the sentences phrased as promises. It is pooled once, in three tiers, so a formal commitment outranks a campaign slogan without either being thrown away:

🤝 Pledge ×3

An explicit commitment in their own words, or a tracked promise in the ledger. Highest confidence.

🧭 Position ×2

A stated, sourced stance. Not a promise, but unambiguous about where they stand.

📣 Branding ×1

A signature issue they campaign on. Low weight, deliberately not zero — running on an issue is a claim about yourself.

ACTION is the formal record only — roll-call votes, sponsorships and official acts. Interviews, news coverage and social posts are never treated as action here; blending them in would make the test impossible to fail. Each tested item comes back ✓ backs it up, ⚠ went against it, ◑ mixed, or … limited evidence, straight from the Official Record's own verdict for that issue — this read classifies nothing on its own.

The number

The percentage is the weighted average of the tested items' outcomes — each item's outcome score times its tier weight, times up to 3× more for how many separate acts judged it, divided by that same total weight. So thirty votes on a hard pledge move it more than one vote on a slogan. Untested word is never scored as agreement or disagreement; it is listed as untested.

It fails closed

A read needs at least 3 tested items and 4 total weight before any percentage exists. Below that there is no number and no verdict — the profile says the coverage is too thin, rather than resting a confident "backs it up" on a single vote. A profile with three tested positions and one with thirty do not get the same confident-looking figure, and the coverage line says which you are reading.

A position is never its own test

Many documented positions are written from the record ("Voted no on H.R. 8", cited to the House Clerk). Scoring those against the same roll call would return 100% for everyone, forever. They stay on the profile as positions and are excluded from the number.

Nothing is counted twice

At most one scored item per issue. Branding is dropped on any issue a stronger item already holds, and a promise promoted to the pledge tier still occupies exactly one slot. An issue with votes but no documented word produces nothing at all — silence is not a position.

🤝

How Pledge Receipts Are Counted

⚠ Retired metric

PolitiDex no longer publishes a Promise % anywhere — not on profiles, cards, comparisons, ballots or share images. Two percentages competing for the same reader made it unclear what was being rated. There is now one graded read: ⚖️ Word vs Action, which checks each stated position against that politician's own roll-call votes. Promises still count — they appear as Kept / Broken / Pending receipts and feed the read above — but they are reported as counts, not a rate. The formula below is kept on the record because it is what the retired number meant.

The retired formula
Promise % = Kept ÷ (Kept + Broken)
× 100 · Pending promises were excluded until resolved · no longer displayed anywhere
Example: John Curtis
31
Kept
6
Broken
3
Pending
31 ÷ (31 + 6) = 31 ÷ 37 = 83.8% → rounded to 78% (Final score incorporates editorial weighting for promise significance — see below)
Scoring Rules
1

Only verifiable public promises count. Vague statements ("I'll do better"), aspirational goals, and unofficial remarks are not scored. Every scored promise must have a source citation.

2

Pending promises are excluded until they can be evaluated as Kept or Broken. This prevents gaming the score by making many vague, unresolvable pledges.

3

Editorial significance weighting is applied for major flagship promises (like "Mexico will pay for the wall") which carry more weight than minor procedural pledges. Weightings are documented per promise in each profile.

4

Partial credit (🔵 Partial) is recorded separately for promises that were partially fulfilled — e.g., a law passed but significantly watered down from what was pledged. Partials count as 0.5 Kept.

5

Scores update in real time as new submissions are verified. A politician's score may change as pending promises resolve or new evidence surfaces about past claims.

Pledge receipts — the "No Record Yet" rule

Receipts only exist once a promise has actually resolved — been counted Kept or Broken. Until then there is nothing to report, so every display path shows “—” / “No record yet” (or “tracked, none resolved yet”) rather than a hollow figure. This matters most for 2026 candidates and brand-new officeholders: an all-pending record earns no read at all. The rule lives in _pdxHasPromiseRecord(), applied everywhere the lane is rendered so it can never be gamed by making many unresolvable pledges.

Last verified Jul 2026 · Example figures reflect John Curtis's tracked promise record at the time of writing; the live score updates automatically as promises resolve.

Data Sources

PolitiDex pulls from a layered stack of primary and secondary sources. Every scored promise requires at least one Tier 1 or Tier 2 source citation.

● Tier 1 — Primary Sources
  • →Official congressional voting records (congress.gov, GovTrack)
  • →State legislature and governor's office records
  • →Official campaign websites and platform documents
  • →C-SPAN transcripts and archived floor speeches
  • →Federal Register and state gazette publications
  • →FEC and campaign finance filings
● Tier 2 — Verified News
  • →PolitiFact Promise Tracker (cross-referenced)
  • →Associated Press, Reuters, NPR
  • →Salt Lake Tribune, Deseret News (Utah coverage)
  • →FactCheck.org and Washington Post Fact Checker
  • →OpenSecrets (campaign finance analysis)
  • →Ballotpedia candidate and election records
● Tier 3 — Community Submissions
  • →Public submissions via the Submit Evidence form
  • →Must include a Tier 1 or Tier 2 source citation
  • →Reviewed by editorial board before scoring
  • →Community upvotes signal priority for review
✕ Never Accepted
  • →Social media posts without corroboration
  • →Partisan blogs or explicitly ideological outlets
  • →Anonymous tips without verifiable evidence
  • →Satire, parody, or out-of-context clips
🎚

Evidence Strength — How Every Badge Is Scored

Every item in the Evidence Locker carries a Strong · Moderate · Limited badge. The badge measures how verifiable a piece of evidence is — not whether we agree with it. It is computed live by _strength(), and every badge lists the plain-language reasons behind it, so it never reads as a black box.

The base score — starts at 0, add points
Official government record — floor video, committee video, or a bill record+2
High-quality direct interview on YouTube (see exception)+2
On-the-record statement or audio+1
Generic YouTube clip / social-media post+0
Direct source link (url)+1
Pinpoint timestamp+1
Tied to a tracked issue (issueKey)+1
●●●
Strong
4+ points
●●○
Moderate
2–3 points
●○○
Limited
below 2
The YouTube interview exception

Most YouTube items are a social/video source and cap at Moderate — a clip is easy to take out of context. But a direct, on-the-record, long-form interview is often the clearest statement of where someone actually stands, so a qualifying interview is graded like a first-person record (+2). It is an explicit, author-set flag, never an automatic guess — marked only when all four hold:

  • 1.Direct — the politician personally speaks, not a clip about them.
  • 2.Attributable — verifiably the named person (confirmed live via YouTube oEmbed).
  • 3.Substantive — a genuine policy discussion, not a soundbite or ad.
  • 4.Long-form — a town hall, podcast, debate, or sit-down (≥ 8 minutes when a length is declared).
Worked examples
●●●Strong · 5 pts

A committee-hearing video (+2 official) with a direct link (+1), a timestamp to the exchange (+1), tied to a tracked issue (+1).

●●●Strong · 4 pts

A 42-minute Iowa PBS interview marked interview:{minutes:42} (+2 interview exception), direct link (+1), tied to an issue (+1). Badge reads: “In-depth direct interview (~42 min, in their own words).”

●●○Moderate · 2 pts

A short campaign clip on YouTube (+0) with a direct link (+1) and an issue tag (+1). A cut-down clip can never be promoted to Strong.

●○○Limited · 1 pt

A social-media post (+0) with a link (+1) but no timestamp and no tracked issue.

Last verified Jul 2026 · Point values and thresholds above mirror the shipped _strength() function exactly.

Verification Process

Every submission goes through a multi-step review before it affects any politician's score. Speed is never more important than accuracy.

01
Submission Received

A contributor submits evidence with the politician's name, verdict, the exact promise or claim, and a source URL. All fields are required. The submission enters a pending queue — not visible publicly until reviewed.

02
Source Verification

Our volunteer research team independently verifies the cited source, confirms the exact promise quote, and checks for context — ensuring nothing is taken out of context or mischaracterized. Turnaround: 24–72 hours.

🤖 MULTI-AI CROSS-VERIFICATION

Editorial team uses multiple leading AI models — Grok, Claude, GPT-4o, Gemini, and others — for initial fact-cross-referencing and context analysis before human review. Discrepancies between models trigger escalated human review.

🔍 Grok 🔍 Claude 🔍 GPT-4o 🔍 Gemini
03
Community Voting

Verified submissions go to public community voting (👍 / 👎). High-upvote submissions are prioritized for editorial review. Community consensus helps surface the most credible and significant catches.

04
Editorial Board Decision

A 3-person editorial panel reviews the submission, the source, community votes, and the full context. They assign a final verdict (Kept / Broken / Partial / Pending) and significance weight. Majority vote rules; dissents are logged.

05
Score Update & Appeals

Approved submissions update the politician's score in real time. Politicians' staff, researchers, or community members may submit an appeal with new evidence. Appeals are reviewed within 7 days. Reversals are possible and publicly noted.

Our Neutrality Promise

"PolitiDex holds every politician to the same standard, regardless of party, ideology, or popularity. A broken promise is a broken promise whether it comes from the left, the right, or anywhere in between."

✓
Equal Treatment

Republicans, Democrats, Libertarians, Independents — all held to identical scoring standards. No exceptions, no favoritism.

✓
No Advertising

PolitiDex does not accept political advertising, PAC funding, or payments from campaigns. Our scores cannot be bought.

✓
Open to Challenge

Anyone — including politicians' own offices — can submit an appeal with new evidence. We correct errors publicly and promptly.

✓
Transparent Scoring

Every score is built promise-by-promise with a full audit trail. Click any politician's profile to see every data point behind their number.

✓
Nonpartisan Editorial Board

Our volunteer editors include politically diverse members — no party may hold a majority on any panel reviewing any single submission.

✓
Conflict of Interest Policy

Editors must recuse themselves from reviewing submissions about politicians they have personal ties to. Recusals are logged and publicly visible.

Writing Standard — The Person, Not the Party

PolitiDex evaluates politicians as individuals, on their own record — not as members of a party. Every Spotlight item, promise, issue position, and summary must answer one question: “What did this person actually do, say, vote for, sponsor, or publicly support?” We never substitute what a party did for what the individual did.

✓ Do
  • “Maloy publicly promoted $45M in rural-broadband funding for her district.”
  • “Passed 14 bills in the 2025 session — among the most of any legislator.”
  • “It passed the House 58–14 and was signed by the governor.”
✕ Don't
  • “She championed funds from a law her side opposed.”
  • “Passed 14 bills — more than any other Democrat.”
  • “It passed the House 58–14 on party lines.”

We avoid partisan-grouping language — “her side,” “his allies,” “the party line,” “like most in his party.” A vote count is a fact; “on party lines” is editorializing, so we state the count. Party context appears only when a person genuinely breaks with their party's prevailing position — because that contrast is part of their own record — and even then the focus stays on the individual.

The “Why it matters” on any item explains the significance of the individual's record — consistency, candor, follow-through, rhetoric vs. reality — never party conflict. We never make a politician a proxy or “barometer” for a party, wing, or movement. Full standard: CONTENT_STYLE.md.

🎯

How We Organize Issues

Every stance, evidence item, and Alignment pick speaks one shared vocabulary: the ISSUE_MAP. Each entry pairs a plain-language label (e.g. 💰 Cut Income & Business Taxes) with a one-line description and keyword set. Tagging a promise or a piece of evidence with an issueKey is what lights up the Stance-at-a-Glance grid, the connected-evidence chips, and the Alignment tool — no extra wiring.

For federal profiles, those keys roll up into twelve Core National Issues, ordered by 2026 salience. A politician “covers” a core issue when any documented stance or evidence is keyed to one of its component keys. The framework is additive metadata — it never changes how an individual stance is written or scored.

1. Economy & Cost of Living
2. Immigration & Border
3. Healthcare Costs & Access
4. Spending, Debt & Waste
5. Abortion / Repro. Rights
6. Gun Rights & Control
7. Climate & Energy
8. Crime & Public Safety
9. Election Integrity
10. Education & Parents
11. Civil Rights & Culture
12. Foreign Policy & Security

Source of truth: CORE_NATIONAL_ISSUES in alignment-tool.js. The Evidence Locker shows each federal profile an X/12 core issues footprint.

🖥

Worked Example — The Data-Center Facet Family

Real records are rarely a single up-or-down opinion. Utah's data-center boom is the clearest case: a legislator can welcome the jobs and demand water and power guardrails at the same time. Rather than flatten that into one “pro” or “anti” label, we split the topic into three flat issue keys — the dc facet family — so the tension shows up as data, not as an editorial caveat.

🖥 Data Centers & AI Growth — datacenter_growth

Welcome data-center and AI investment for the jobs, tax base, and competitiveness it brings.

💧 Data Centers & Water — datacenter_water

Require proof they won't drain scarce water or the Great Salt Lake — closed-loop cooling, no ag-to-industrial water grabs.

⚡ Data Centers, Power & Ratepayers — datacenter_power

Make them bring their own clean power and pay their own way, so family utility bills and air quality don't take the hit.

The polarity rule

On the water and power keys the label states the protective position. So a card's issueStance:'support' means pro-safeguard, 'oppose' means “let them draw or burn freely,” and 'mixed' means “backs the project with conditions.” This lets one honest record read pro-growth yet water- and power-skeptical at once — exactly how many Utah officials actually stand.

Last verified Jul 2026 · The three dc facet keys are confirmed against the live ISSUE_MAP vocabulary.

Corrections & “Last Verified” Provenance

Getting it wrong and quietly leaving it is not an option. Anyone — a voter, a journalist, or a politician's own office — can flag an error, and corrections are handled in the open.

1
Anyone can appeal

Submit new evidence through the Submit Evidence form. Appeals are reviewed within 7 days.

2
Reversals are public

When a verdict changes, the change is noted rather than silently overwritten. Editorial dissents are logged.

3
Not retroactive by stealth

Major methodology changes are announced and are not applied to existing scores without review.

4
Sourced, always

A correction has to clear the same source-tier bar as the claim it replaces.

“Last verified” provenance

Every profile carries a lightweight provenance trail — when its record was last touched and how much is tracked — so a number is never presented as timeless. Records that resolve on a live check (for example, a YouTube interview's existence and attribution confirmed via YouTube's oEmbed endpoint) reflect the moment of that check. If a profile looks thin or stale, that is shown honestly rather than dressed up as complete.

Disclaimer

Estimates

All Word vs Action reads, pledge verdicts and Accountability Scores are estimates based on publicly available information and editorial judgment. They are not legal findings, official government assessments, or definitive verdicts. Reasonable people may disagree on how to score any individual promise or position.

Accuracy

We strive for accuracy but cannot guarantee that all information is complete, up-to-date, or error-free. Political records are complex, sometimes contradictory, and subject to interpretation. If you find an error, please submit a correction via our appeals process.

Not Legal

Nothing on PolitiDex constitutes legal advice, defamation, or a formal accusation of wrongdoing. All statements about potential conflicts of interest are based on public reporting and are presented as information for civic discussion, not as established fact.

Updates

This methodology may be updated as PolitiDex grows and our processes improve. Major methodology changes will be announced publicly and will not be applied retroactively to existing scores without review.

Welcome to

PolitiDex

A free, nonpartisan way to see what politicians actually do — not just what they say. PolitiDex helps you look past left vs. right and judge the people on your ballot by integrity, follow-through, and how well they match your values.

Don't judge them by their party. Judge them by their record and your values. One figure — Direction Match: what they said, measured against the votes and official acts on file. It publishes only where the record runs deep enough to test; where it doesn't, we say so instead of guessing. Matching your own values is a separate tool, and it's yours alone.
